title: Compiling Loop-Based Nested Parallelism for Irregular Workloads
problem: Nested parallel loops incur significant overheads from task creation and management that can eliminate parallelism benefits. Programmers must manually tune code to balance parallelism gains against these costs, particularly challenging for irregular, input-sensitive workloads where performance depends on input characteristics.
motivation: Manual tuning of parallel code requires understanding hidden architectural factors like task scheduling and load balancing, which is extremely difficult for irregular workloads.
method: HBC is a compiler that translates C/C++ programs written with fork-join parallelism (instructions that let different code sections run simultaneously, like OpenMP) into optimized machine code. It uses Heartbeat Scheduling to automatically control task granularity—how much work each parallel task completes before yielding—with formal performance guarantees, meaning we can mathematically prove that management overhead won't eliminate parallelism benefits. The compiler adjusts task granularity dynamically based on actual runtime data patterns, so irregular, input-sensitive workloads (where performance depends on what data the program receives) can benefit from parallelism without requiring programmers to manually tune the code.
key_novelty: HBC is the first compiler to automatically translate fork-join parallelism (parallel code sections, including those nested within other parallel sections) into machine code that adjusts task granularity (work per parallel piece) with formal performance guarantees, eliminating manual tuning for irregular workloads.
contributions: HBC compiler for automatic translation of high-level fork-join parallelism constructs
Integration of Heartbeat Scheduling with formal performance guarantees for automatic granularity control
Automatic adaptation to irregular, input-sensitive workloads without manual programmer tuning
Outperforms both OpenMP and entirely manual solutions for balancing parallelism and task overhead
